title: The Great Rift Valley
summary: How two tectonic plates slowly pulling apart carved a huge valley across East Africa, filled it with deep lakes and volcanoes, and may someday split the continent in two.
poll: A landscape that looks solid and unchanging today could actually be slowly transforming over millions of years.

versions.title: A Giant Crack in the Land
versions.text:
Can the land crack open? Yes! That makes a rift.

The top of the Earth is a hard skin. It is the crust. The crust is cut in big parts. Each part is a plate. The plates move. They move as slow as your nails grow.

Two plates pull apart. The land between them stretches. Then it sinks down low! This makes a long, deep valley. A crack runs down each side.

The valley is in East Africa. It is called the Great Rift Valley. You can see it from way up in space.

Some lakes sit deep in the valley. A few are some of the deepest lakes on Earth. Tall mountains stand near it too.

Hot rock can push up inside a mountain. Over time, this can make a volcano.

Our land is on a plate, too. It moves away from Africa. So the Red Sea gets a bit wider each year.

No one knows how wide the rift will grow. But geologists watch it. One day, it may split Africa in two.

versions.title: The Crack That Keeps Growing
versions.text:
Most of the time, the land looks still. But in East Africa, the ground is slowly cracking apart. This is called a rift.

The top of the Earth is a hard, rocky layer. It is called the crust. The crust is cut into huge parts called plates. The plates move all the time. They move as slow as your nails grow.

In East Africa, two plates pull apart. The land between them stretches. It gets thin. At last, a long strip of land sinks down. This leaves a deep valley. A crack, called a fault, runs along each side.

The valley starts deep in the crust. On top, it forms the long Great Rift Valley. The valley is so big you can see it from way up in space.

Most of the valley is quiet and still today. But deep lakes have filled parts of its floor. A few of these lakes are among the deepest lakes on Earth.

Tall mountains and volcanoes rise near the edges of the valley. Hot melted rock can push up through cracks and slowly build a volcano.

Saudi Arabia sits on its own plate. It moves slowly away from Africa. That is why the Red Sea grows a bit wider each year. Geologists watch the ground here with care.

No one can tell how wide the rift will grow. But scientists study it closely. One day, the rift may widen enough for the sea to rush in.

versions.text:
Most of the time, the ground beneath our feet seems perfectly solid and dependable. In East Africa, however, the land itself keeps tearing slowly apart: a long, deep valley grows a little wider every single year. This ongoing process is called rifting, and the Great Rift Valley it has produced is one of the most striking geological features on our planet.

The outer layer of the Earth, known as the crust, consists of hard rock that is fractured into enormous sections called plates. These plates fit together like the pieces of a gigantic puzzle, and they are constantly moving, although extremely slowly. They creep along at roughly the same speed that human fingernails grow.

In East Africa, two plates meet along what is called a divergent boundary, where the plates pull steadily apart instead of pushing together. The land caught between them stretches and grows thinner, much like dough being pulled apart at both ends. As the crust thins, long cracks called faults appear along either side, and the strip of land between them gradually sinks, forming a deep trench bordered by steep walls called escarpments.

The rift begins deep underground, at the point where the two plates first start pulling apart. On the surface, the trench stretches for thousands of kilometers through Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania, and it is usually deepest and widest near its middle.

The vast majority of the valley floor sits quiet today, but deep lake basins have formed there over millions of years. Several of these rift lakes rank among the deepest lakes found anywhere on Earth.

Tall mountains and active volcanoes rise along the escarpments. Molten rock called magma forces its way upward through the thinning crust, and gradually, layer by layer, it constructs a volcano.

Saudi Arabia occupies its own continental plate, which is gradually diverging from Africa along the Red Sea. As a consequence, the Red Sea becomes slightly wider every year, part of the very same rifting system that produced the valley in East Africa.

Geologists who study this rifting system believe it offers a preview of Africa's distant future, when the surrounding sea may finally flood in and divide the continent into two separate landmasses.

versions.title: The Great Rift Valley: A Crack That Keeps Growing
versions.text:
Most of the time, the ground beneath our feet seems perfectly solid and dependable. Occasionally, however, geologists note a far slower disturbance: in East Africa, a long valley keeps widening year after year, undetected by anyone standing on its floor. This ongoing disturbance is called rifting, and it ranks among the most significant geological processes on our planet.

The outer layer of the Earth, known as the crust, consists of rigid rock that is fractured into enormous sections called tectonic plates. These plates interlock like the pieces of a gigantic puzzle, and they are perpetually in motion, although extraordinarily slowly; geologists calculate that they creep along at approximately the same speed at which human fingernails grow.

In East Africa, two tectonic plates meet along what geologists term a divergent boundary, where the plates pull steadily apart rather than pushing together. Because the crust between them is stretched repeatedly, it grows progressively thinner, much like dough being pulled apart at both extremities. Eventually, lengthy fractures known as faults emerge along either margin, and the intervening strip of land gradually subsides, forming a deep trench flanked by steep rocky walls termed escarpments.

The rift originates deep underground, at the precise location where the two plates first begin diverging, and on the surface the resulting trench extends for several thousand kilometers through Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania, remaining deepest and widest near its middle.

Although the overwhelming majority of the valley floor remains quiet from one day to the next, deep lake basins have gradually formed there across millions of years. Several of these rift lakes rank among the deepest documented anywhere on Earth.

Tall mountains and active volcanoes rise along the escarpments flanking the rift. Molten rock termed magma forces its way upward through the thinning crust, and gradually, layer upon layer, it constructs a volcanic peak.

Saudi Arabia occupies its own continental plate, which is gradually diverging from the African plate along the line of the Red Sea. As a consequence, the Red Sea becomes fractionally wider every year, forming part of this very same rifting system responsible for the valley in East Africa.

Geologists who study this rifting system maintain that it offers a preview of Africa's distant future, an era when the surrounding sea may eventually flood inward and divide the continent into two distinct landmasses.

versions.title: The Great Rift Valley: A Crack That Keeps Growing
versions.text:
Earth's outer shell is divided into enormous tectonic plates that drift across the planet's surface at a pace so slow it rivals the growth rate of a human fingernail, an almost imperceptible motion that nonetheless reshapes the planet over geological time. In East Africa, two such plates meet along a divergent boundary, pulling apart rather than colliding, a process called rifting that stretches and thins the crust caught between them until it can no longer resist the strain.

As the crust thins along this divergent boundary, long fractures called faults open along either margin, and the strip of land between them slowly subsides, forming a long, deep trench bordered by steep walls called escarpments. This trench, the Great Rift Valley, extends for thousands of kilometers through Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania, and is visible even from orbit as a winding scar across the continent, its course tracing the boundary between the two slowly diverging plates.

Earthquakes sometimes accompany this slow stretching, as stress stored in the rock is suddenly released along a fault. Scientists measure these events using seismometers, instruments sensitive enough to detect ground movement too faint for anyone to feel directly. Over millions of years, deep lake basins have formed along the rift's floor, several ranking among the deepest lakes on the planet, while rising magma along its edges has slowly built volcanic peaks layer by layer, one eruption after another.

Saudi Arabia occupies its own tectonic plate, one that is gradually separating from the African plate along a similar divergent boundary, a process actively widening the Red Sea over long timescales. In recognition of this ongoing activity, geologists study the Afar region of Ethiopia, where the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the East African rift all meet at a single triple junction, offering a rare view of several stages of continental breakup within one small area, and helping them understand how divergent boundaries evolve elsewhere on Earth.

Geologists cannot yet predict the exact moment the rift will finally widen enough for the sea to flood in, but their continuous monitoring steadily improves estimates of how the region will change. Communities living near this slowly widening rift must balance ordinary daily life with the knowledge that the ground beneath them, however solid it feels, is never truly at rest. Scientists argue that this patient, ongoing observation remains the best way to understand a landscape that is still, quite literally, in the process of being born, one almost imperceptible movement at a time, shaped by forces that will keep reshaping it long after today's rivers, lakes, and volcanoes have themselves changed beyond recognition.

versions.title: The Great Rift Valley: A Crack That Keeps Growing
versions.text:
Earth's outer shell is divided into enormous tectonic plates that drift across the planet's surface at a rate so gradual it rivals the growth of a human fingernail, an almost imperceptible motion that nevertheless reshapes the planet's geography over sufficiently long timescales. In East Africa, two such plates meet along a divergent boundary, diverging rather than colliding, a process geologists term continental rifting, which progressively stretches and thins the crust trapped between them until that crust can no longer withstand the accumulated strain.

As the crust continues thinning along this divergent boundary, long fractures known as faults open along either margin, and the intervening strip of land gradually subsides, producing an extensive trench bordered by steep escarpments. This trench, known collectively as the Great Rift Valley, extends for several thousand kilometers through Ethiopia, Kenya, and Tanzania, remaining visible even from orbital altitude as a winding scar traversing the continent, its course closely tracing the boundary between the two slowly diverging plates beneath it.

Earthquakes occasionally accompany this gradual stretching, as accumulated stress within the rock is abruptly released along a fault line. Scientists quantify these events using seismometers, instruments of sufficient sensitivity to detect ground movement far too subtle for any person to perceive directly. Across millions of years, substantial lake basins have accumulated along the rift's floor, several ranking among the deepest lakes documented anywhere on the planet, while magma rising persistently along its margins has gradually constructed volcanic peaks layer upon layer, eruption after eruption, across vast stretches of geological time.

Saudi Arabia occupies its own distinct tectonic plate, one that is gradually separating from the adjacent African plate along a comparable divergent boundary, a slow geological process actively widening the Red Sea across extended timescales. In recognition of this persistent underlying activity, geologists study the Afar region of Ethiopia with particular intensity, where the Red Sea, the Gulf of Aden, and the East African rift all converge at a single triple junction, offering a rare and valuable glimpse of several distinct stages of continental breakup within one remarkably compact area, and informing how scientists interpret divergent boundaries elsewhere in the world.

Geologists cannot yet predict the exact moment at which the rift will finally widen sufficiently for the sea to flood inward, but their continuous, meticulous monitoring steadily refines estimates of precisely how the region is likely to change. Communities inhabiting this slowly widening rift must therefore balance the routines of ordinary daily life with the persistent awareness that the ground beneath them, however solid it may feel underfoot, is in fact never truly at rest, a condition that scientists argue makes patient, sustained scientific observation the most practical means of understanding a landscape that remains, quite literally, still in the process of being born, continually reshaped by forces operating far too slowly for any single human lifetime to witness their ultimate conclusion.

wrong.C: The article does not compare African lakes to every lake elsewhere.
wrong.D: The article says the valley can be seen from space.

wrong.C: Lakes form slowly over millions of years, not instantly.

wrong.C: Rain is not described as unique to rift valleys.

MID.prompt: Explain the steps that create the Great Rift Valley, from moving plates to the finished trench. Use at least three steps in order.
checklist: I explained at least three steps in order.
I used words from the article such as tectonic, fault, and trench.
I used order words like first, then, and finally.
MID.modelAnswer: First, two tectonic plates in East Africa slowly pull apart. Then, the land between them stretches and thins until cracks called faults appear on each side. Finally, the strip of land between the faults sinks down, forming a deep trench. Over time, lake basins and volcanoes form along the rift.

keyWords.definition: describes two things, such as tectonic plates, moving steadily away from each other
keyWords.example: The two paths were divergent, leading hikers in opposite directions.

keyWords.definition: hot melted rock found below Earth's surface
keyWords.example: Magma cooled and hardened into solid rock after it reached the surface.

keyWords.definition: a long, steep slope or cliff that separates two areas of different height
keyWords.example: Climbers used ropes to reach the top of the rocky escarpment.

keyWords.definition: having to do with a continent or its large plate of crust
keyWords.example: A continental plate can carry both land and parts of the seafloor.

keyWords.definition: a scientist who studies rocks, land, and how Earth changes
keyWords.example: The geologist collected rock samples from the mountainside.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the central idea of the article?
options: Volcanoes never form near divergent plate boundaries, anywhere on Earth.
Continental rifting stretched and dropped the crust between divergent plates.
Lakes only form in deserts, never in rift valleys, in the whole world.
Geologists have proven the rift valley will close within a decade or so.
questions.why: The article explains that divergent plates slowly stretched and dropped the crust between them, forming the rift valley along with its lakes and volcanoes.

wrong.A: Volcanoes do form near the rift's divergent boundary.
wrong.C: Deep lakes are described as forming inside the rift valley, not deserts.
wrong.D: The article says the rift may widen over millions of years, not close.

questions.stem: In the article, what does the word "divergent" mean?
options: Moving steadily toward each other
Staying perfectly still
Moving steadily away from each other
Spinning in a circle

wrong.A: Divergent plates move apart, not toward each other.
wrong.B: The plates are described as moving, not staying still.
wrong.D: Spinning is not mentioned; the plates pull apart in a steady direction.

wrong.B: Windblown sand is not part of volcano formation in the article.
wrong.C: Melted ice is not mentioned in the article.

questions.stem: Why does the continental crust between the two plates eventually subside?

wrong.A: Meteors are not mentioned in the article.
wrong.B: Magma rising builds volcanoes; it does not cause the crust to subside.
wrong.D: Geologists study the rift; they do not dig under it.

questions.stem: What does the Afar triple junction suggest about East Africa's future, according to the article?

That the rift will close completely within a few years

That the plates there will suddenly stop diverging

wrong.C: Rising magma continues to build volcanoes along the rift.
wrong.D: The plates are described as continuing to diverge, not stopping.

questions.stem: Why does the author compare the Afar region to a preview of East Africa's future?

To prove that continents never change shape

wrong.A: An escarpment is a wall-like landform, not a lake.
wrong.C: Escarpments are not described as volcanoes.
wrong.D: Escarpments are landforms, not measuring tools.

questions.stem: How is the formation of the Red Sea similar to what may someday happen to the East African rift?

Both are found on a different planet

wrong.C: Volcanoes are a result of rifting, not its sole cause.
wrong.D: Both the Red Sea and the East African rift are on Earth.

HIGH.prompt: Is the Great Rift Valley likely to keep changing in the future, or has it already finished forming? Support your answer with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
checklist: I supported it with at least two pieces of evidence from the article.
I explained how my evidence connects to my opinion.
HIGH.modelAnswer: I think the Great Rift Valley will keep changing because the article explains that the divergent plates are still slowly pulling apart today. Geologists studying the Afar triple junction believe the rift may someday widen enough for the sea to flood in, splitting the continent, much like the Red Sea already split away from Africa. Since this process is ongoing rather than finished, the rift is still actively forming.
